procedural_history.impugned_order: Common order dated 26th October, 2007 passed by the High Court of Bombay at Goa in Criminal Revision Application Nos. 3, 10, 19, 21 and 22 of 2007.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court set aside the charges framed by the Special Judge, Panaji against the accused-appellants for offences punishable under Sections 120-B, 409, 420, 465 and 471, IPC and directed to frame charges against them under Sections 13 (1)(d)(i) and 13(1)(d)(ii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 read with Section 120-B, IPC.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (originally the accused) filed Criminal Appeals by way of special leave against the High Court's order.

directions: Liberty is granted to the counsel for the appellants to place before the trial Court, the material, judgments and the earlier passed order of this Court which are referred before the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in upholding the trial court's decision to frame charges against the appellants, particularly when it was argued that the case was based on mere suspicion and that a prior civil ruling by the Supreme Court on the same notifications should have led to the termination of proceedings.

facts: The appellants were charged with offenses under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and the Indian Penal Code.

The core allegation was that two government notifications were issued in 1996 without proper Cabinet approval and in violation of rules, resulting in wrongful gains for certain companies and a loss to the public exchequer.

The appellants argued that the case was based on mere suspicion and that a prior civil ruling by the Supreme Court concerning the same notifications should have led to the dismissal of the criminal case.
law: The Supreme Court reiterated the legal standard for framing charges under Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The standard is to determine if a 'prima facie' case exists. A prima facie case is made out if the evidence is sufficient to make a prudent person believe that the alleged facts probably existed or happened.

At the stage of framing charges, the court cannot conduct a 'roving enquiry' into the pros and cons of the matter or weigh the evidence as if it were conducting a full trial. The evaluation is limited and not a detailed examination of the merits.
application: The Court reviewed the facts in a 'holistic manner' and concluded that, prima facie, a case could be made out against the appellants.
It specifically noted the allegation that the notifications were issued without Cabinet approval and in violation of rules as a key factor.
The Court determined that it was not necessary to conduct a 'thorough examination of merits' at this preliminary stage, as the issue was only about framing charges.
It concluded that the material on record was sufficient to obligate the lower courts to frame the charges, and therefore, there was no error in their decision.

Regarding the prior civil ruling, the Court did not quash the proceedings on that basis but granted the appellants the liberty to present that judgment and other materials before the trial court for its consideration during the trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' arguments and upheld the High Court's decision to frame charges. The Court reasoned that the allegations and the material on record were sufficient to establish a prima facie case, which is the only legal requirement at the charge-framing stage. A detailed examination of the evidence, including the impact of the prior civil ruling, was a matter for the trial itself, not for a preliminary hearing on charges.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in upholding the trial court's decision to frame charges against the appellants, particularly when it was argued that the case was based on mere suspicion and that a prior civil ruling by the Supreme Court on the same notifications should have led to the termination of proceedings.
appellant_arguments: A prior Supreme Court order in a civil appeal dealing with the same notifications should lead to the termination of the current criminal proceedings.
The charges are based on mere suspicion, which is not a sufficient ground for framing charges.
The complaint was previously closed and only reopened due to the political will of the complainant after he came to power.
One appellant, a subordinate official, was merely acting on instructions from superiors in the normal course of his duties and was not a deciding authority, so he cannot be considered a conspirator.
The allegation that an appellant was 'close to the Minister' is not a valid ground for levelling charges.
No benefit was actually received by the appellants from the notifications, and any amount that had to be paid has already been paid.
respondent_arguments: There was enough prima facie material on record to establish that the accused public servants entered into a criminal conspiracy with company officials to facilitate wrongful gains for the companies.
The accused abused their official positions in pursuit of the conspiracy, causing a huge loss to the public exchequer and illegally benefiting the companies.

One of the accused prepared a false document, giving it the appearance of a genuine one, to deceive the government into making a policy decision that granted a 25% rebate on power supply to the accused companies.
The High Court correctly found that there was sufficient prima facie material to frame charges against all the accused.

cases.case_name: State by the Inspector of Police, Chennai v. S. Selvi and Ors.
cases.principle: At the stage of framing charges, the court should apply a prima facie standard and cannot conduct a roving enquiry into the pros and cons of the matter or weigh the evidence as if it was conducting a trial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When framing charges under Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court must apply a prima facie standard. A prima facie case is established when the probative value of the evidence concerning all essential elements of the charge, taken as a whole, is sufficient to induce the court to believe in the existence of those facts or to consider their existence so probable that a prudent person would act on that supposition. At this stage, the court cannot conduct a roving enquiry into the merits of the matter or weigh the evidence as if it were conducting a trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Upon reviewing the record and the sequence of events in a holistic manner, the Court concluded that a prima facie case can be made out against the appellants, as the material on record obligated the framing of charges. The Court specifically noted the allegations that the notifications in question were issued without Cabinet approval and in violation of rules, and determined that a thorough examination of the merits was unnecessary and inappropriate at the stage of framing charges.
legal_tests_applied: At the stage of framing charges, there cannot be a roving enquiry into the pros and cons of the matter and the court cannot weigh the evidence as if it was conducting a trial.
why_appellant_lost: The Court determined that, prima facie, a case could be made out against the appellants, thus rejecting the argument that the charges were based on mere suspicion. The specific allegation that the notifications were issued without Cabinet approval and in violation of rules was sufficient to proceed.

The Court explicitly declined to conduct a detailed examination of the case's merits, stating it was inappropriate at the charge-framing stage. The Court noted, "we do not think it necessary to go into the aspect of thorough examination of merits of the case, particularly when the issue is still at the stage of framing of charges only."
The Court found no error in the High Court's decision, concluding that "presumably the material on record obligated the Court to" frame the charges.
why_respondent_won: The Court agreed with the respondent's position that there was sufficient prima facie material to frame charges, stating, "prima facie, it cannot be said that no case can be made out against the accused— appellants."

The Court accepted that the allegations regarding the improper issuance of the notifications were a key factor in establishing a prima facie case, noting, "Allegedly, the Notifications dated 15-5-1996 and 1-8-1996 were issued without the approval of Cabinet and by violation of rules."
policy_considerations: The Court's reasoning reinforces the legal principle that the stage of framing charges involves a limited inquiry, not a full-scale evaluation of evidence. The refusal to conduct a "thorough examination of merits" at this point is a systemic consideration to ensure the proper progression of a criminal trial, where evidence is to be weighed and tested.
